blocks.text: Chapter 7.
Overfitting: When to Think Less
Seventh night, friend — and it opens with police officers in a real gunfight... pausing, mid-firefight, to pick up their spent brass casings and put them in their pockets.

Why on earth? Because on the firing range, that's what they'd always done — fire, then collect your brass. Practice had burned the incidental detail in alongside the essential one. FBI agents drilled to fire two shots and reholster were found reholstering in actual gunfights. These men weren't badly trained, friend. They were too perfectly trained — flawlessly adapted to the exact structure of the practice environment, and fragile the moment reality differed from it.

Statisticians have a name for this disease, and tonight's chapter makes an outrageous claim: the same disease explains why more thinking, more factors, and more data can make your decisions worse — and why, in the right circumstances, the truly rational move is to think less.
The nine-factor trap

Plot a handful of data points — say, life satisfaction against years of marriage — and fit curves. A simple one-factor line catches the broad trend. A nine-factor polynomial passes through every single point perfectly... and then swings wildly between and beyond them, predicting absurdities. That model has the lowest error on the data you have and the highest error on any data you'll ever see next. This is overfitting, friend: the flexible model doesn't just learn the relationship — it memorizes the noise, the sampling flukes, the quirks of this particular dataset. And noise doesn't repeat. Every real dataset is signal plus noise, so chasing a perfect fit is — in the authors' lovely phrase — idolatry of data: worshipping the measurements instead of the thing they imperfectly measure.

And the disease is everywhere once you see it. Your taste buds are a model overfit to a vanished world: sugar and fat were honest signals of scarce calories on the savannah — then the food industry gamed the proxy, delivering the taste divorced from the nutrition. Organizations overfit whenever they optimize the metric instead of the goal: reward arrest counts and you get arrests, not safety; judge schools by test scores and you get teaching-to-the-test, not learning. The detection tool is cross-validation: hold back data the model never saw — or check a second, independent proxy for the same goal. If test scores rise while an unannounced alternate test stays flat, the system has overfit the metric. Cheap, rotating spot-checks, friend — random audits beside official reports — are how you catch a proxy the moment it decouples from reality.
Making complexity pay rent

Prevention is more elegant than detection: make complexity expensive. Regularization charges every factor a penalty, forcing it to justify its place by improving the fit more than it costs. The celebrated Lasso drives marginal factors' weights to exactly zero — deleting them — leaving a short list of variables that genuinely matter. Nature runs her own Lasso, friend: metabolism charges calories for every neuron, so only complexity that pays for itself survives. And the human version is a hard budget on your own deliberation: Charles Darwin, deciding whether to marry, confined the entire question to one page — children and companionship against lost time and "less money for books" — ruled on the spot ("Marry—Marry—Marry Q.E.D."), proposed to Emma Wedgwood, and lived happily. The single page was a Lasso for the mind.

Pause and guess: Harry Markowitz won the Nobel Prize for portfolio optimization — the exact mathematics of ideal investment allocation. So when he invested his OWN retirement savings... how did he split the money?
Ready? Here is what happened.

Fifty-fifty. Stocks and bonds. Straight down the middle. The Nobel laureate of optimal allocation used the naive equal split — and here's the glory of it, friend: the math later vindicated him. Research found the simple 1/N portfolio — equal amounts in everything — frequently outperforms the fitted "optimal" portfolios on new data, because estimating optimal weights from limited history means overfitting historical noise. The pattern generalizes powerfully: Robyn Dawes showed that improper linear models — skip the fitting, weight every factor equally — predict about as well as fully optimized regressions across domains. His famous example: marital stability is well predicted by rate of lovemaking minus rate of arguments — no fitted coefficients at all. And Gerd Gigerenzer went further: fast and frugal heuristics like Take the Best — decide on the single most valid cue, ignore everything else — can beat multiple regression on real data. Heuristics aren't the lamentable shortcuts of a limited brain, friend. They're natural regularization, tuned for a world of scarce, noisy data — where ignoring information is the statistically correct thing to do. The greater the uncertainty, the simpler you should go.
Quit while you're ahead
The last tool regularizes with time itself.

Pause and guess: Train a neural network and track its accuracy on FRESH data — not the training data — as learning proceeds. The curve does something surprising partway through. What — and what's the remedy?
Ready? Here is what happened.

Accuracy rises... peaks... and then FALLS as training continues. Early in training the network learns the broad, real structure; keep going and it starts absorbing the noise. The remedy is called early stopping: quit at the peak — regularization implemented in time. And human deliberation follows the same curve, friend: the factors that come to mind first are usually the most important; extended rumination dredges up progressively more marginal considerations and weighs them ever more finely — fitting the noise in your own evidence. That's the algorithmic diagnosis of the chronic overthinker and the perfectionist: not the opposite of a lazy thinker — an overfitter. The prescription is conditional, not blanket: when data is plentiful and clean — a stable, well-understood domain with reliable feedback — think long; complexity earns its keep. But when evidence is scarce, noisy, or drawn from a world that may not resemble the one you'll act in — career choices, relationships, forecasts years out — weigh the few factors you're confident about, resist elaborating, and stop early. Franklin's moral algebra, Darwin's single page, the rough plan shipped over the perfect one: all early stopping. Thinking less, in the right circumstances, isn't a failure of rationality, friend. It is rationality.
Before you go

So: officers pocketing brass mid-gunfight and palates craving a vanished savannah — perfect adaptation to the wrong world; the nine-factor fit that predicts nothing; cross-validation to catch a gamed proxy; the Lasso and Darwin's one page making complexity pay rent; the Nobel laureate who split fifty-fifty and was right; and the training curve that commands you to quit at the peak. This week, friend: one decision, one page, five factors maximum — and rule when the page is full.

But a monster waits in tomorrow's chapter, friend. Some problems aren't just hard — they're provably unsolvable in any reasonable time: the traveling salesman with his exploding map, the seating chart from hell. And yet computer scientists solve them every day — by cheating beautifully: relaxing the rules until the impossible turns tractable, and — strangest of all — by rolling dice on purpose. Next time: relaxation and randomness — solving the unsolvable.
Key takeaways
Overfitting: matching your data too well means memorizing noise — lowest error on the past, highest on the future.
Proxies come apart under pressure: taste buds, test scores, arrest counts — optimize the metric hard enough and it stops measuring the goal.
Cross-validate: hold back data or check an independent second measure — a gamed proxy fails the test it wasn't coached for.
Regularize: charge complexity rent — the Lasso zeroes out marginal factors, and Darwin's one-page limit did the same for a marriage decision.
With scarce, noisy data, simple wins: equal weights (Dawes), single best cue (Gigerenzer), and the 1/N portfolio that beat the Nobel math.
Early stopping: first factors are the real ones — overthinking is overfitting, and quitting at the peak is the rational move.
